title: Social Media Strategy
subtitle: How to plan and talk about your company's presence on social media
description: Learn the key words for social media marketing — how to describe your strategy, measure results, and talk about content, reach, and engagement.
dialogueSubtitle: Riley presents Brightline's social media strategy to Dana

vocabulary.definition: The number of people who interact with your content — for example: likes, comments, and shares.
vocabulary.example: Our engagement rate went up by 30% after we started posting video content on LinkedIn.

vocabulary.definition: The number of different people who see your content.
vocabulary.example: Our reach on Instagram doubled after we used more relevant hashtags.

vocabulary.definition: The number of times your content is shown — including when the same person sees it more than once.
vocabulary.example: We had 50,000 impressions on our last LinkedIn post, but only 3,000 of those were unique people.

vocabulary.definition: A word or phrase with a # symbol, used on social media to group content by topic.
vocabulary.example: We use three to five hashtags on each post to help more people find our content.

vocabulary.definition: A person who has a large following on social media and can promote a product or brand to their audience.
vocabulary.example: We worked with an influencer in the B2B marketing space — her audience is exactly our target market.

vocabulary.definition: Anything you post on social media — a photo, video, article, or text.
vocabulary.example: We post a mix of content — tips, case studies, behind-the-scenes posts, and product updates.

vocabulary.definition: A social media app or website — for example: LinkedIn, Instagram, or TikTok.
vocabulary.example: LinkedIn is our main platform because our target audience is marketing professionals.

vocabulary.definition: Data and numbers that show how your social media content is performing.
vocabulary.example: We check our analytics every Monday to see which posts performed best last week.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Grow a group of followers who regularly see and interact with your content.
phrasalVerbs.example: We built an audience of 8,000 followers on LinkedIn over two years by posting consistently.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Share content on a regular schedule — not just when you feel like it.
phrasalVerbs.example: The key to social media growth is to post consistently — three times a week, every week.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Create content that makes people want to like, comment, or share.
phrasalVerbs.example: Questions and polls drive more engagement than simple product posts.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Spread very quickly across social media — seen by a very large number of people in a short time.
phrasalVerbs.example: One of our LinkedIn posts went viral last year — it got 200,000 impressions in three days.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Pay to show a social media post to more people beyond your existing followers.
phrasalVerbs.example: We boosted the post on LinkedIn to reach marketing managers who do not follow us yet.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Monitor the analytics to see how well your content is doing.
phrasalVerbs.example: We track performance every week — reach, engagement, and clicks are the three key numbers.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Riley, can you walk me through Brightline's social media strategy? I want to build a better one for my agency.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Of course. First, we decided which [[platform:a social media app or website]] to focus on. For us, LinkedIn is the main one because our audience is marketing professionals.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: And how do you decide what [[content:anything you post — a photo, video, article, or text]] to post?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: We post a mix — tips, case studies, behind-the-scenes, and product updates. The key is to post consistently. If you stop for two weeks, your [[reach:the number of different people who see your content]] drops quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: What is the difference between reach and [[impression:the number of times your content is shown]]s?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Reach is how many different people see your post. Impressions include every time the post is shown — so if the same person sees it three times, that counts as three impressions but only one person in reach.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: And [[engagement:the number of people who interact with your content — likes, comments, and shares]]? Is that more important than reach?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: I think so. A post can have high reach but low engagement — which means people saw it but did not care. Engagement shows that your content is actually interesting to your audience.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Do you use [[hashtag:a word with a # symbol used to group content by topic]]s?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Yes — three to five per post. More than that looks spammy on LinkedIn. We choose hashtags that our target audience follows.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Have you worked with an [[influencer:a person with a large following who can promote your brand]]?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Yes — once. A B2B marketing influencer shared one of our posts. It reached a completely new audience. We look at our [[analytics:data and numbers that show how your content is performing]] every Monday to track what is working.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: This is very helpful. I think I need to focus on LinkedIn and post more consistently.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: That is the biggest thing. Consistency builds an audience. Start with two posts a week and track the performance. You will start to see what your audience responds to.

chooseResponse.instructions: Work in groups. Read the question or comment. Talk about which response (A, B, or C) is best. Choose together, then click to check.

items.customerLine: Which social media platform should we use?
options: All of them — you need to be everywhere.
It depends on your audience. For B2B marketing, LinkedIn is the strongest platform — that is where your target audience spends their professional time.
Facebook is the biggest, so you should start there.
items.explanation: B is correct. Platform choice should be based on where your audience is — not which platform is biggest or easiest. For a B2B marketing audience, LinkedIn is the right answer.

items.customerLine: Our posts get lots of views but very few likes or comments. Is that okay?
options: Yes — views are the most important thing.
That is good reach but low engagement. It means people are seeing the content but it is not making them want to interact. Try asking a question or sharing a strong opinion — that drives engagement.
It means the algorithm does not like your content.
items.explanation: B is correct. It explains the problem clearly — high reach, low engagement — and gives a practical tip. A ignores the engagement issue. C blames the algorithm without giving any useful advice.

items.customerLine: Should we use hashtags on LinkedIn?
options: Yes — use as many as possible so more people find you.
Yes, but keep it to three to five relevant hashtags. More than that looks spammy on LinkedIn. Choose ones that your target audience actually follows.
No — hashtags are for Instagram, not LinkedIn.
items.explanation: B is correct. It gives a specific, practical answer — three to five, and make sure they are relevant. A gives the wrong advice. C is incorrect — hashtags work on LinkedIn too.

items.customerLine: How do we know if our social media strategy is working?
options: We check the analytics — reach, engagement, and clicks — every week. We look at which posts performed best and do more of what works.
We look at how many followers we have.
If people are talking about us, it is working.
items.explanation: A is correct. It names the specific metrics to track and explains what you do with the data. B only looks at one metric. C is too vague and hard to measure.

profileMatch.instructions: You are Riley. Three companies want to improve their social media. As a group, decide what each company should focus on first. Click 'Check Matches' when you agree.

profiles.name: A company with good content but almost no followers
profiles.description: A B2B software company posts great content three times a week, but they only have 200 followers. Almost nobody sees their posts.

profiles.name: A company with many followers but no interaction
profiles.description: A company has 5,000 followers on LinkedIn. Their posts get many views but almost no likes, comments, or shares.

profiles.name: A company that posts whenever they feel like it
profiles.description: A marketing agency posts sometimes — two posts in one week, then nothing for three weeks. Their follower count is not growing.

options.label: Increase reach
options.description: Try boosting posts to reach people who do not follow you yet, use relevant hashtags, and consider working with an influencer in your space to introduce the brand to a new audience.

options.label: Drive engagement
options.description: Change the type of content you post — ask questions, share strong opinions, or post polls. Content that makes people think or react will drive more likes, comments, and shares.

options.label: Post consistently
options.description: Set a schedule — for example, two posts per week — and stick to it. Consistency is the most important thing for growing an audience. Posting once and then disappearing kills momentum.

finishTheLine.instructions: The marketer's line is not finished. As a group, discuss how you would finish it. Use vocabulary from this lesson. There is no single correct answer — compare your ideas, then click to see one example.

items.customerLine: What is your social media strategy?
items.salespersonStart: Our main platform is LinkedIn. We post three times a week — a mix of tips, case studies, and behind-the-scenes content. We track our analytics every Monday and look at
items.suggestedCompletion: reach, engagement, and clicks. We also boost the best-performing posts to increase our reach beyond our current followers.

items.customerLine: How do you choose what to post?
items.salespersonStart: We look at our analytics to see what type of content gets the most engagement. Posts that ask a question or share an opinion always perform well. We post a mix of
items.suggestedCompletion: educational content, like tips and how-to posts, and more personal content, like behind-the-scenes or team updates. The variety keeps the audience interested.

items.customerLine: Have you ever worked with an influencer?
items.salespersonStart: Yes — once. We identified a B2B marketing influencer whose audience matched our target market. She shared a post about our product and
items.suggestedCompletion: our reach doubled that week. We saw a big increase in new followers and website visits. It was a low-cost way to reach a new audience very quickly.

items.customerLine: What does a good social media strategy look like?
items.salespersonStart: A good strategy starts with choosing the right platform for your audience. Then you decide how often to post and what type of content to create. You track the
items.suggestedCompletion: analytics regularly — reach, impressions, and engagement — and adjust based on what is working. Consistency is the most important part. Without it, your audience does not grow.
